profiles.meeting_scenario: A troubleshooting meeting in an ML research lab trying to explain why an internal replication of a paper on biologically plausible orthogonal initialisation is failing on a deep feedforward benchmark. The lab has a codepath that reproduces the recurrent results, but the feedforward runs still show gradient instability or only weak improvement, despite everyone believing they already used the paper's orthogonalisation scheme. The agenda is to diagnose whether the issue comes from how the orthogonalisation phase was implemented, which checkpoint was evaluated, what counts as 'stable gradients,' and whether the method was applied to the intended part of the model. The expected outcome is a concrete rerun plan and a shared diagnosis of the likely source of the discrepancy.

members.name: Dr. Lena Ortiz
members.expertise: Theoretical deep learning, dynamical isometry, biologically motivated learning rules
members.background: Lena led the lab's reading group on biologically plausible initialisation methods and is preparing a replication note comparing theory claims with actual training behavior in recurrent and feedforward networks.
members.private_state: She wants a faithful reproduction of the paper's mechanism before the lab dismisses the method, and she is worried that implementation shortcuts are being mistaken for a failure of the theory.
hidden_assumptions: A 'pre-training orthogonalisation' phase is a separate offline procedure that runs before any supervised objective is introduced.
An 'orthogonalized checkpoint' means the final snapshot after the orthogonality criterion has converged, not an early intermediate save.
If gradients are 'stable,' the relevant evidence is near-isometric Jacobian behavior at initialization, even before ordinary training begins.
For the feedforward theorem to map to practice, orthogonalisation is meant for the hidden weight matrices, not automatically every linear layer in the model.

members.name: Arun Mehta
members.expertise: Training infrastructure, experiment management, PyTorch implementation, large-scale debugging
members.background: Arun maintains the lab's unified training pipeline and integrated the paper's biologically plausible orthogonalisation routine into the existing experiment framework used for both recurrent and feedforward models.
members.private_state: He wants to keep one maintainable codepath for all model families and is trying to avoid bespoke preprocessing stages that complicate scheduling, checkpointing, and logging.
hidden_assumptions: A 'pre-training orthogonalisation' phase can be implemented as a warm-up stage inside the normal training loop as long as it occurs before the model fully settles into task learning.
An 'orthogonalized checkpoint' is the saved artifact from the orthogonalisation-tagged stage of the run, typically the first stable checkpoint produced by the pipeline.
If gradients are 'stable,' the practical test is that training avoids NaNs, clipping spikes, and erratic loss during the first part of optimization.
When a method is described as applying to the feedforward network, it is natural to include all linear layers under the same config flag unless explicitly excluded.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say they already used 'pre-training orthogonalisation.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means a standalone orthogonalisation process completed before supervised training starts, with no task-loss updates mixed in.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means an initial warm-up segment inside the normal training run where the orthogonality objective is active alongside the existing training machinery.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase sounds standard and both implementations happen early in the run, so each person hears confirmation rather than a need to unpack whether 'pre-training' is offline or in-loop.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say they want to check whether the method 'fixes gradient instability' or yields 'stable gradients.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 judges stability by initialization-time signal propagation properties such as Jacobian singular values or layerwise gradient norm preservation before task learning distorts the picture.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 judges stability by whether the first training segment runs smoothly in practice, without NaNs, severe clipping, or visibly erratic loss curves.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In troubleshooting conversations, 'stable gradients' is a natural shared phrase, and both standards are professionally legitimate enough that neither sounds suspicious on the surface.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to 'the orthogonalized checkpoint' from the feedforward run.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of the final snapshot after the orthogonality objective has effectively converged and the weights are closest to the intended orthogonal state.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of the pipeline's saved checkpoint labeled with the orthogonalisation stage, which is the early step-500 artifact with the '_ortho' suffix.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: There is only one prominently named artifact in the dashboard, so both believe they are referencing the same file even though one is using the label semantically and the other operationally.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree the method should be applied to 'the feedforward network' or 'the whole model.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes this includes only the hidden-layer weight matrices relevant to the theoretical analysis and signal propagation argument.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes this includes every linear layer covered by the implementation flag, including the classifier head and any projection layers.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: At a high level, both descriptions sound equivalent because the head is still part of the model, and neither expects this boundary choice to be important enough to state explicitly in a short status discussion.

We already said we did pre-training orthogonalisation, but to me that means a distinct offline procedure that finishes before any task-loss learning starts. If that got blurred into ordinary optimization, then a negative result doesn't tell us much about the theory.
